Diskutiere mit Freunden über Steuersätze, Umweltverschmutzung, Infrastrukturprojekte und warum Paul schon wieder den halben Wald abgeholzt hat.

Eco ist eines dieser Spiele, die auf Bildern komplett harmlos aussehen und dann plötzlich dein Leben übernehmen. Am Anfang schlägst du ein paar Bäume um und baust eine kleine Hütte. Eine Woche später arbeitest du in einer funktionierenden Wirtschaft, handelst mit anderen Spielern und regst dich darüber auf, dass die Straße zum Nachbardorf immer noch nicht fertig ist.

Im Singleplayer macht das Spiel schon Spaß, aber auf einem Server mit anderen Leuten wird es komplett verrückt. Da entstehen plötzlich echte Berufe. Einer ist Holzfäller, einer Bergarbeiter, einer Koch und irgendein Typ verdient mehr Geld als alle anderen zusammen, weil er zufällig als Erster eine wichtige Fähigkeit gelernt hat.

Das Beste ist, dass jede Entscheidung Konsequenzen hat. Wenn alle nur auf Profit gehen, ist irgendwann die Umwelt kaputt. Wenn niemand wichtige Berufe übernimmt, steht die gesamte Wirtschaft still. Und trotzdem schafft es immer irgendwer, eine völlig unnötige Diskussion über Steuern oder Straßenbau anzufangen, die länger dauert als der eigentliche Bau.

Irgendwann merkt man, dass man nicht mehr spielt wie in anderen Survival-Games. Man baut nicht einfach irgendwas hin. Man plant. Man rechnet. Man organisiert. Und plötzlich fühlt man sich wie Bürgermeister, Unternehmer und Bauarbeiter gleichzeitig.

10/10

Eco is a pretty slow-moving game, but it’s also one of the most unique games I’ve played. It takes that idea of “build a community where everyone has a role and relies on each other,” which a lot of games have tried and failed to do, and somehow actually pulls it off.

It doesn’t just simulate a town. It simulates a full economy, settlements, politics, governments, and eventually entire countries. You start off with basic professions like logging, mining, or campfire cooking, then slowly work your way into better technology as people specialize into different roles. Certain professions are the only ones that can make certain things, so if you want metal tools, you need a blacksmith. That kind of system makes everyone feel important in a way most games never really manage. It scratches a very specific itch: roleplay, but without having to pretend.
That being said, Eco definitely has its problems. The biggest one is the time commitment. Once you get invested, it can start feeling like a second job. A lot of players seem to drop off after the first week or so, even though most servers are built around a 30 to 45 day run. The main goal is to stop a meteor from wiping out the planet, usually after 30 real-life days. To get there, everyone has to work together, build up technology, create infrastructure, and manage resources without completely wrecking the environment along the way.

I really love Eco. Though it's biggest downfall is that just there isn't enough people playing it. The community can feel small, and you’ll definitely start recognizing the same names, but the game itself is something special. There really isn’t much else like it.

I'm making this a negative review because there are some things about the game I didn't like, even though I didn't really manage to get into it properly. I just want to get the developers' attention, in case they can change something.

I'll start with calories and crafting. I can see how they grow in an insane progression, with brutal consumption between tiers. Personally, I ended up a hunter/cook and a gatherer/farmer so I could provide everything for myself, since it's more profitable for a farmer to make seeds for oil rather than corn. And this ties into yet another problem with the game. A person would do thousands of crafts and spend thousands of calories over a few hours. One person alone ate a whole day's worth of the bison population, chased it all down with rice porridge, and tried to maintain a balanced diet out of a couple hundred meals a day.

I also don't understand the calorie system as a concept. I'd take meat, cut it, then shape it and fry it. Each ingredient and the end result have different calorie counts. Or take salads, for example, making them on a campfire versus a cast-iron stove: the difference is at least 5x in ingredients, but the calorie difference isn't even 2x.

Another thing I didn't like is that ingredients ultimately boil down to some universal base. On a campfire I can make a ton of different salads, but on the stove I can make 2 salads, each in 3+ different ways.

Personally, I had animals flying, teleporting, running in circles, and disappearing. Might have been an issue specific to our server, but I'm going to mention it anyway.

Animal and plant reproduction is kind of weird. I don't know, maybe it's just configured that way. But for instance, I noticed there were fewer than 100 corn plants, so I planted them in different places, and only some chosen ones started reproducing, even though I planted all the bushes in the best conditions.

I actually really liked the game, especially playing it with a big group so that everyone gets their own profession and the political and economic systems work to their full potential. Not 5 people trying to save the world.

En grosse communauté, les villes deviennent vite injouables.
Les mods n’aident pas, au contraire : la plupart sont encore plus mal optimisés que le jeu de base.

Pour faire rapide :

CPU bound de fou (calculs économie + voxels + physique simplifiée)
Mal multithreadé
Et surtout → serveur dépendant
(si le serveur rame → toi tu rames)

La communauté…

Je passe le côté politique, mais globalement :
Peu d’entraide réelle, ca force dessus mais c'est au final très 'macro' aide (potes / intérêt indiv)
Des comportements égoïstes (je fais n’importe quoi a coté de chez toi, mais ne fais pas la même chose chez moi)
Des critiques permanentes pour rien (“t’as vendu trop cher”, “t’as tout acheté”, etc.)
Ou des "ouin ouin" parce que ta piqué 5 melons sur une terre pas revendiqué.

Tu as toujours, quelqu’un qui construit n’importe comment, qui "crée" des mines dégueulasses, des routes absurdes, ou des joueurs ultra no-life qui avancent 10x plus vite que toi, rendant ton métier inutile si tu joues normalement (2–3h par soir).

En rapide : 

“t’as acheté trop de bois”
“t’as cassé le marché”
“cette route est illégale”
“vote pour taxer machin”

👉 + les no-life :

20h/jour
contrôlent un métier entier
bloquent toute progression normale

Les serveurs

Probablement le pire point :

Début correct, puis à partir du jour 2 ou 3 → c’est la catastrophe
Lag, freeze, actions qui mettent 5 à 15 secondes à se faire.
Jouer devient une punition, surtout avec certains mods.

Conclusion

Le jeu peut être sympa :
👉 en petit groupe (4–5 joueurs)
👉 avec une bonne organisation
👉 peu de mods
👉 et sans constructions trop ambitieuses

Mais même dans ces conditions, le jeu reste techniquement dépassé, notamment graphiquement.

I find the premise very interesting and I found the town aspect super intriguing & unique as well. In many multiplayer survival games, I love to make a town or create a store to engage with other players, so this was a very promising aspect of the game to me. Making towns or shops in other games isn't always perfectly integrated and doesn't guarantee traffic, it is often just seen as a novel little RP thing to engage in. But with this game having it be a crucial mechanic seemed really cool and downright promised engagement in this type of stuff. However, the game proved to be tedious and frustrating in many aspects.

[h3]BUILDING & FURNISHING:[/h3]
The economy and town building works out decently  - but the first thing I find disappointing is the balance around building mechanics. As a person who loves building I was very disappointed with the sheer amount of unreal grind you have to put up just to get some cool construction materials. Mortar/hewn materials were bearable... But once it was time for "tier 3" (bricks), the grind just became unreal. It gets better later down the line, but I still personally found it incredibly tedious to do a substantial amount of town building in our smaller server (unless you like ugly box houses). 

It's also silly how inconsistent the building blocks are. Some of them have less blocks to choose from, some of them have more. Some connect their walls/fences automatically, some don't. You can't even rotate some of the blocks (walls, from what I remember). The painting mechanic was really disappointing too. It's just glorified screenshots, unless I'm missing something. I was hoping to run a little shop where I make custom shop signs or other requests, but it's not possible.

[h3]OVERALL PROGRESSION:[/h3]
After a week or two of playing on a 10 person server, progression came to a halt. Everyone got confused and tangled up in their businesses, beginning to take all sorts of specializations and just doing everything and nothing at once. For a while I wasn't sure if we're just bad or if the game failed to convey something to us. Ultimately, I just feel like it isn't balanced very well towards smaller groups - there are config settings for this, but a new group of players will not know how to tweak them accordingly (and I don't think the default settings do the game any justice). In mid-game, a new player group will typically get lost in setting up political positions (that will be able to organize progress and funds for the said progress) long enough for people to get discouraged and bored of the server. 

[h3]CONCLUSION: [/h3]
I think the game requires some fine tuning. A pretty decent foundation is laid down, but a lot of things need to be rebalanced or polished. I think the game needs to communicate a bit better how important political positions are. It also needs to cater towards smaller groups better. Specializations could use some streamlining. Also, more QoL for crafting or inventory management would be handy (better sorting options, automatic distribution to chests, more compact menus).

Aside from that, it's a cool unique game, worth a try if you have a few spare bucks - as long as you have a ton of time to dump and someone who actually knows this game well. Perhaps this works better on a full server, or a group with 15+ people.
